title: Tao Yuanming, 'Drinking Wine' no. 5
short: The fifth of Tao Yuanming's twenty poems 'Drinking Wine' (Yin jiu), in Waley's 1918 version, printed untitled.
body: Tao Qian, also called Tao Yuanming (365-427), served briefly in minor offices and then retired, in 405, to farm near Mount Lu in modern Jiangxi; he became the model of the recluse-poet for all later Chinese literature. 飲酒 Yin jiu, 'Drinking Wine', is a set of twenty five-character poems, which his preface says he wrote when drunk on long autumn evenings. No. 5 is the most famous of them and perhaps of all his poems. Waley, who calls Tao 'the greatest of these recluses', prints it in A Hundred and Seventy Chinese Poems (1918) without a title, using his first line instead, and renders each Chinese line as one long unrhymed English line.

title: 'among men' (ren jing 人境)
short: Tao does not live in remote mountains: he builds his hut among other people, yet hears no noise of the world.
body: 結廬在人境，而無車馬喧, 'I built my hut in the human realm, yet there is no clamour of carriage and horse'. 人境 ren jing, 'the human realm', is literally 'the boundary/region of men', which Waley renders with the bureaucratic-sounding 'zone of human habitation'. The 'carriages and horses' are those of officials and visitors, the traffic of ambition and social life. The paradox, recluse not in the wilds but amid ordinary life, distinguishes Tao from the 'mountain hermits' of earlier tradition: reclusion is a state of mind.

title: 'when the mind is far, the place becomes remote'
short: The poem's answer to its own question: a mind detached from the world makes its own solitude.
body: 問君何能爾？心遠地自偏, 'you ask how this can be? With the heart far away, the place becomes remote of itself'. The question-and-answer form, with the poet addressing himself as 'you' (君), introduces a philosophical note. 心遠 'heart/mind distant' is the key idea, related to Daoist and Buddhist ideals of a mind free from attachment. Waley's 'creates a wilderness round it' is a vivid expansion of 地自偏, 'the place is naturally out of the way'; 'wilderness' adds a sense of wild nature not in the Chinese, where the place is merely secluded.

title: chrysanthemums under the eastern hedge
short: Chrysanthemums are autumn flowers of longevity, drunk in wine at the Double Ninth festival; through this line they became Tao's emblem.
body: 采菊東籬下, 'plucking chrysanthemums by the eastern hedge'. The chrysanthemum blooms in late autumn, after other flowers fade, and was thought to prolong life; its petals were steeped in wine for the Double Ninth festival (ninth day of the ninth month). Tao's poems mention it repeatedly, and after him the chrysanthemum and the 'eastern hedge' became shorthand for the recluse's life and for Tao himself. The eastern hedge places the flowers in his own garden: the scene is domestic, not wild. The plucking may be for wine, linking the image to the series title.

title: 'see' (jian 見) or 'gaze at' (wang 望) the Southern Mountain?
greek: 悠然見南山 / 望南山
short: Su Shi argued that Tao 'sees' the mountain by chance, not 'gazes' at it; Waley's 'gaze long' follows the rejected sense.
body: The received text reads 悠然見南山, 'carefree, I see the Southern Mountain'. Some editions read 望 wang, 'gaze at'. Su Shi (1037-1101) insisted on 見 jian: the mountain comes into view while the poet is picking flowers, so that scene and mind meet without intention; to read 'gaze' would make the poem lose all its spirit. His judgement helped fix the received text, and Xiaofei Tian's study of Tao's manuscript transmission is a good introduction to how readers' images of Tao shaped his text. Waley's 'gaze long' reads 悠然 youran ('leisurely, far-reaching') as 'long', and makes the looking deliberate, the very reading Su Shi rejected.

title: the Southern Mountain (Nanshan): Mount Lu
short: The Chinese names the 'Southern Mountain', probably Mount Lu near Tao's home; Waley's 'summer hills' clashes with the autumn chrysanthemums.
body: 南山 Nanshan, 'the Southern Mountain', is usually identified with Mount Lu (Lushan), south of Tao's home near Xunyang. The phrase also echoes the Shijing, where 'the Southern Mountain' is a figure of permanence and long life ('like the longevity of the Southern Mountain', Mao 166), so it suits the chrysanthemum's associations of longevity. Waley's 'the distant summer hills' replaces the specific mountain with a generalised landscape; 'summer' is odd, since chrysanthemums bloom in autumn, and may reflect his reading of 南, 'south', associated in Chinese cosmology with summer. 'Distant' renders the sense of 悠然.

title: evening mountain air
short: 'The mountain mists are lovely at sunset': the Chinese 'air' (qi) is the mist or vapour that rises at dusk.
body: 山氣日夕佳, 'the mountain air at sunset is fine'. 氣 qi, 'breath, vapour, air', here refers to the hazy atmosphere round the mountain at evening, which Tao sees as beautiful (佳 jia). Waley's 'fresh' changes a visual impression to one of touch or smell. Dusk also marks the end of the day and, by implication, of life, a time for return.

title: birds returning at evening
short: Birds flying home at dusk are a figure of Tao's own 'return' from office to his fields, the central theme of his work.
body: 飛鳥相與還, 'flying birds return together'. 相與 means 'together, in company', and Waley's 'two by two' adds an image of pairing not specified in the Chinese. 'Return' (還 huan) links the line to Tao's famous prose-poem 'Homeward Bound' (歸去來兮辭, 405), where the clouds drift out of the hills and 'the birds, weary of flying, know to return'. The birds embody a natural rhythm the poet has rejoined by leaving office. Compare Waley's version of 'Returning to the Fields' (tao-chien/8) in this archive.

title: 'true meaning' (zhen yi 真意)
short: The scene holds a 'true' meaning, zhen being the Daoist word for the authentic, unspoiled nature of things.
body: 此中有真意, 'in this there is a true meaning'. 真 zhen, 'genuine, true, authentic', is a key Daoist term, used in Zhuangzi for the original nature that society corrupts; 真意 is the real significance of the scene, or of the life it represents. Waley's 'deep' interprets rather than translates 真. The poem does not say what the meaning is, which is its point.

title: 'I want to explain it but have already forgotten the words'
short: The last line alludes to Zhuangzi's fish-trap parable: once the meaning is grasped, the words can be forgotten.
body: 欲辨已忘言, 'I wish to explain it, but have already forgotten the words'. The phrase 忘言 wangyan, 'forget words', recalls Zhuangzi ch. 26: the fish-trap exists for the fish, the snare for the hare, words for meaning; 'once you have got the meaning, you forget the words', and Zhuangzi longs for someone who has forgotten words to talk with. Tao's line thus claims a wordless understanding at the end of a poem. Waley's 'words suddenly fail us' makes it a failure of expression rather than a forgetting after understanding, and his 'us' generalises the poet's 'I' (implied in the Chinese).
